parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 16. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a pet care company to ask about having her cat looked after while she is away. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Daniel: Good morning, Paws at Home Pet Care. Daniel speaking. Rachel: Oh, hello. I'm going away for a couple of weeks next month, and I need someone to look after my cat while I'm gone. A friend told me you do home visits. Daniel: That's right. We come to your home once or twice a day, so your pet can stay somewhere familiar. Is it just the one cat? Rachel: Yes, just one. He's called Biscuit. He's three years old and very friendly. Daniel: Lovely. Well, our basic visit package takes about half an hour. The sitter feeds the cat, gives fresh water and washes the food bowls. They also clean the litter tray every time, and they spend some time playing with the cat, so it doesn't get lonely. Rachel: That sounds fine. Is brushing included? He has quite long fur. Daniel: The sitter can give him a quick brush if he'll let them, yes. That's part of the basic visit. Then there are some extra services you can add if you want. Some people like us to put their lights on in the evening, for example. Rachel: No, I've got timers for the lights, so there's no need for that. But could the sitter bring in the post every day? I don't want a pile of letters behind the door. It makes it obvious that nobody's at home. Daniel: Yes, of course. We can do that on every visit. And what about the curtains? Some customers ask us to open them in the morning and close them again at night. Rachel: Oh, yes, please. That would be good, for the same reason. Daniel: OK. And do you have any house plants that will need watering? Rachel: No, my neighbour's going to deal with the plants and the garden. She's offered to do that. Daniel: Fine. Then there are the weekly jobs. Would you like the sitter to put your bins out for collection? Rachel: Yes, please. They're collected on Tuesday mornings, so they need to go out on Monday evening. Daniel: No problem. Anything else we could do once a week? Rachel: Well, I've also got a small fish tank in the kitchen. The fish get fed by an automatic feeder, so that's all right. But the filter in the tank needs cleaning once a week. Is that something you could do? Daniel: Yes, our sitters can clean the filter. I'll make a note of that. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Daniel: Now, there are a few other things we can offer that you might find useful. If Biscuit became ill while you were away, we could arrange for a vet to visit him at home. A lot of cats get very stressed if they're put in a basket and taken to a surgery. Rachel: That's good to know. He hates travelling. What if something happened to the house, though, like a leak? Daniel: We'd contact you straight away, of course, and your sitter would call a plumber if you wanted them to. We also offer an overnight service, where one of our sitters actually stays in your home. That's mostly for pets that are elderly and shouldn't be left alone for long periods, especially at night. Rachel: Right. Well, Biscuit's still young, so I don't think he needs that. Can I ask a bit about the sitters themselves? I'll be giving someone my keys, after all. Daniel: Of course. All our sitters go through a careful selection process. They have an interview, and we take up two references from previous employers. Every sitter also has a qualification in animal welfare, which covers things like spotting the early signs of illness. Rachel: That's reassuring. And what happens if something gets broken in the house? Daniel: Well, all our sitters are fully insured, so you'd be covered for any accidental damage. It very rarely happens, though. Rachel: Good. And how will I know how things are going? Will the sitter phone me? Daniel: We don't usually phone, because customers are often in a different time zone. Instead, the sitter sends you a short report by email after each visit, with a photo of your pet. People really like that. Rachel: Oh, that's a nice idea. And will it be the same person every time? Daniel: Yes, we try to keep the same sitter for the whole booking, and we nearly always manage it. Rachel: Great. Well, I'd like to go ahead and book, then. Daniel: Wonderful. Can I start with your name, please? Rachel: Yes, it's Rachel Dunmore. That's D, U, N, M, O, R, E. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a consultant talking to a group of restaurant owners about reducing food waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Good afternoon, everyone. My name's Claire Hollins, and for the past eight years I've been working with restaurants and cafés to help them cut down on the amount of food they throw away. I'm sure you've all seen how much food ends up in the bin at the end of a busy night. And I'm sure most of you would like to see less of it. Speaker: So where does all this waste come from? When I ask restaurant owners, most of them say it's food that goes off in the fridge or the store room before it can be used. Others say it's the trimmings and peelings from preparing vegetables and meat in the kitchen. Both of those are real, of course. But what most owners don't realise is that the biggest share of the waste in a typical restaurant is the food that customers leave on their plates. Speaker: So what does all this waste actually mean for you as owners? Well, some people worry that it'll get them a bad reputation, or that it'll cause problems when the council inspectors come round. In practice, that very rarely happens. The real impact is on your costs. Every plate of food that goes in the bin is food you've paid for, and paid staff to prepare, and then paid again to have taken away. Over a year, that can add up to thousands of pounds. Speaker: So, what can you do about it? First, let's get rid of one very common mistake. Whatever you do, never throw food away simply because it's passed its best before date. That date is about quality, not safety. Food is often perfectly good for some time afterwards, so check it and use it. It's the use by date that you must take seriously, and of course you should always follow the rules on storing food at the right temperature. But far too much good food is wasted because of a misunderstanding about those labels. Speaker: Cutting waste can bring other benefits too, some of which you might not expect. Take The Harbour Kitchen, a seafood restaurant down on the seafront. When they started looking at what was coming back from the tables, they realised their main courses were simply too big, so they reduced the portion sizes. They expected to save money on ingredients, and they did. What they hadn't predicted, though, was that far more diners started ordering a dessert, because they weren't too full to manage one. So their takings per table actually went up. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Now I'd like to give you some examples of restaurants I've worked with recently, to show you some of the different approaches that are possible. Speaker: At The Olive Tree, the owner realised that her staff didn't see food waste as their problem at all. So now, at the end of every evening, the kitchen team weigh the bins themselves and write the figure on a board, and once a month they all sit down together to discuss ideas for bringing the number down. Several of the best ideas have come from the youngest members of staff. Speaker: Café Lumo is a small bakery café in the city centre. They always had bread and cakes left over at the end of the day, which were thrown away. Now a local charity sends a volunteer to collect anything that hasn't been sold, and it's taken to a night shelter for homeless people. The café's waste has dropped enormously. Speaker: The Brasserie used to have a menu with more than forty dishes. That meant keeping a huge range of ingredients in stock, and many of them went off before anyone ordered them. The chef cut the menu down to fifteen dishes that share a lot of the same ingredients, and their waste has fallen by about a third. Speaker: Spice Garden, an Indian restaurant, had a different problem, which was the vegetable peelings and scraps from the kitchen. They now have an arrangement with a community garden near the restaurant. The garden's volunteers collect the scraps twice a week and turn them into compost, and in return, the restaurant gets some of the herbs they grow. Speaker: At the Riverside Grill, lots of customers were leaving large amounts of chips and salad on their plates. So they now offer most of their dishes in two portion sizes, regular and light, and they've also stopped serving side dishes automatically. Customers order them if they want them. Speaker: And finally, The Mill House, where the head chef now runs a short course for every new member of kitchen staff. They learn how to store food properly, how to use every part of a vegetable, and how to turn leftovers into staff meals. Speaker: OK, so now I'd like to move on to look at some of the costs involved. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two product design students called Leo and Hannah talking about Leo's interest in cooking and about a seminar on the history of kitchen equipment. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Hannah: Hi, Leo. So, how are you finding the course so far? Leo: Really well, thanks. Hannah: I've been meaning to ask you. Someone told me you were planning to be a chef when you were at school. Is that right? Leo: That's right. From about the age of fourteen, that was all I wanted to do. I cooked all the time. Hannah: Were you good at it? Leo: Well, everyone in my class seemed to think so. Whenever there was a party, they'd all ask me to make the food, and they'd tell me I should have my own restaurant one day. I loved that, to be honest. Hannah: I'm not surprised. And your family? Did they want you to do something more academic? Leo: No, not at all. My parents were really supportive. My mum used to let me take over the kitchen every weekend. Hannah: So what went wrong? Leo: Looking back, I relied too much on what my friends said. I could make a few impressive dishes, but I never really bothered to learn the basics properly, things like knife skills and making stocks and sauces. I should have spent a lot more time on those. Hannah: Didn't your teachers tell you that? Leo: They probably tried. Anyway, when I was seventeen, I got a place on a work experience scheme in a restaurant in Lyon, in France, for a week. It was a really well-known restaurant. I was so excited before I went. But on the first morning, the head chef asked me to make a simple omelette. He took one look at it, and threw it in the bin in front of the whole kitchen. Hannah: Oh no. How did you feel? Leo: I just wanted the floor to open up and swallow me. My face went completely red. And he was right. It wasn't good enough. Hannah: Were you angry with him? Leo: No, I wasn't angry, it was fair. And actually, during the rest of the week, I got to see how he worked. The kitchen was incredibly busy, but he never raised his voice, and he noticed every tiny detail. I just thought, that's what a real chef is like. I really looked up to him. Hannah: And were you on your own the whole time? That must have been hard. Leo: I thought I'd be lonely, because I didn't know anyone, but the other kitchen staff took me out every evening, so it was fine. And I expected to be bored, because I spent hours peeling vegetables, but there was always something interesting going on around me. Hannah: So is that why you gave up the idea of being a chef? Leo: Partly. I realised I was more interested in how kitchens work, the equipment and the layout, than in cooking itself. That's how I ended up doing product design. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Hannah: Well, that fits in nicely with our seminar next week, doesn't it? We've got to present some ideas on the history of kitchen equipment. Leo: Yes, I've started making some notes. I thought we could begin with the tin can. It was invented in about eighteen ten, so that food could be kept for a long time, especially for soldiers and sailors. Hannah: But how did they open them? Weren't the early cans made of really thick metal? Leo: Yes, and that's the interesting thing. The can opener wasn't invented until nearly fifty years later. Before that, people had to use a hammer and chisel, or a knife, or even a bayonet. Hannah: That's amazing. OK, what about the electric kettle? That must have been a big improvement on boiling water on a stove. Leo: You'd think so. But the first ones, in the eighteen nineties, had the heating element in a separate compartment underneath the water. They took over ten minutes to boil, so a lot of people didn't see the point of them. Hannah: Right. And then there's the fridge. I read that the early electric ones were very expensive. Leo: They were, but the more serious problem was the gases they used for cooling. Some of them were toxic, like ammonia, and if a fridge leaked, people in the house could become seriously ill. Hannah: I didn't know that. What about the microwave oven? Everyone knows the story about the scientist who found that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted, so I don't think we need to go over that. Leo: No. But what I found surprising was the size of the first ones. The first microwave oven, in nineteen forty-seven, was taller than a person and weighed more than three hundred kilos. It was far too big for an ordinary home kitchen. Anyway, what about non-stick pans? Do you know anything about those? Hannah: Yes, I looked them up. The non-stick coating was created in a laboratory in the nineteen thirties. And in the nineteen fifties, a French engineer was using it on his fishing equipment, to stop his lines getting tangled. It was his wife who suggested he try it on her cooking pans. Leo: That's a great story. And were people suspicious of them at first? Hannah: Apparently not. They sold really well right from the beginning. Leo: OK. And one more, perhaps. The dishwasher? Hannah: Yes, the first really practical one was designed in the eighteen eighties by a woman who was fed up with her servants breaking her china. But for a long time, hardly any families had one. They were mostly bought by hotels and restaurants, and it was decades before they became common in people's homes. Leo: Great. I think we've got plenty for the seminar now. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a food science student giving a presentation about the production of vanilla. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Good morning, everyone. In this series of presentations, we've been looking at natural food products, and today I'm going to talk about vanilla. Most of us know it as a flavour, and many people think of it as rather plain and ordinary. We even use the word vanilla in English to mean something boring. But as you'll see, the story of how it's produced is anything but boring. Student: So, what exactly is vanilla? Well, it comes from the long, thin seed pods of a particular kind of orchid. The pods contain thousands of tiny black seeds, and it's these pods, once they've been treated, that give us the flavour. Vanilla is used in ice cream, cakes, chocolate and drinks, of course, but it's also an important ingredient in many perfumes, because of its warm, sweet smell. And it's a valuable crop. In fact, after saffron, vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world, and I'll explain why in a few minutes. Student: Let's start with the plant itself. The vanilla orchid is a climbing vine, which means it can't support its own weight. In the wild, it grows up the trunks of trees, and on farms it's usually trained to climb up trees or wooden posts. It needs a warm, humid climate, with plenty of rain, but it doesn't like too much direct sunlight, so it needs partial shade to grow well. Today, vanilla is grown in several tropical countries, but by far the largest producer is Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, which grows around four fifths of the world's supply. Student: But vanilla doesn't come from Madagascar originally. It was first grown by the Totonac people in what is now Mexico, many centuries ago. They used it as a flavouring and as a medicine, and later the Aztecs used it to flavour a chocolate drink. When the Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, they took vanilla back to Europe, where it quickly became fashionable. Student: Now, in the following centuries, people tried to grow vanilla in other parts of the world. The plants grew perfectly well, and they produced flowers, but they didn't produce any pods at all. Nobody could understand why. The reason, it turned out, was that the insects that pollinated the flowers in Mexico didn't exist anywhere else. Without them, the flowers simply dropped off. Student: The problem was finally solved in eighteen forty-one, on the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, by a twelve-year-old enslaved boy called Edmond Albius. He discovered that he could pollinate the flowers by hand, using a small stick to lift a thin flap inside the flower and then pressing the parts together with his thumb. It was quick and simple, and it worked. Remarkably, this is still the method used on vanilla farms today, almost two centuries later. Student: So let's look at how vanilla is produced now. Vanilla vines usually start to flower about three years after they're planted. The flowers grow in groups, but each individual flower opens for just one day, usually early in the morning. If it isn't pollinated that day, it won't produce a pod, so workers have to check every plant each morning during the flowering season. A skilled worker can pollinate well over a thousand flowers in a day. This is one of the reasons why vanilla is so expensive: almost every pod in the world has been produced by hand. Student: After pollination, the pods take around nine months to grow to their full size. At this stage they're green and have no smell or flavour at all. Farmers wait until the tips of the pods start to turn yellow, and that's the sign that they're ready to be picked. Picking them too early is a common problem, because vanilla is sometimes stolen from the vines, and some farmers harvest early to protect their crop. But unripe pods produce vanilla of much poorer quality. Student: Once the pods have been picked, the curing process begins, and this is what creates the flavour. First, the pods are dipped in hot water for a few minutes, which stops them from ripening any further. Then they're wrapped in blankets and packed into wooden boxes, where they're left to sweat overnight. Over the following weeks, the pods are spread out in the sun for a few hours each day, and wrapped up again each night. Gradually they turn a deep brown colour, and the typical vanilla smell develops. Student: Finally, the pods are dried slowly indoors for several months. Good quality pods are soft and shiny, and sometimes tiny white crystals appear on their surface. These are crystals of vanillin, which is the main flavour compound. Altogether, the process from flower to finished pod can take well over a year, and that's before the vanilla has even left the farm. So that's the basic process. Now, I'd like to look at the market for vanilla. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Which way of reducing food waste was used in each of the following restaurants?

Choose your answers from the box and write the correct letter, A, B or C, next to Questions 15-20.

Ways of reducing food waste
A   changing the food that is offered
B   working with outside organisations
C   training and involving staff

Questions 25-30

What comment do the students make about the early development of each of the following items of kitchen equipment?

Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to Questions 25-30.

Comments
A   It was very slow to work.
B   The material was first used for a different purpose.
C   It needed a tool that had not yet been invented.
D   It could be dangerous to people's health.
E   It was expensive to run.
F   It was too large for most homes.
G   It was mainly bought by businesses at first.
H   Nobody wanted to buy it at first.

And what happens if something gets broken in the house? Daniel: Well, all our sitters are fully insured, so you'd be covered for any accidental damage. It very rarely happens, though. Rachel: Good. And how will I know how things are going? Will the sitter phone me? Daniel: We don't usually phone, because customers are often in a different time zone. Instead, the sitter sends you a short report by email after each visit, with a photo of your pet. People really like that. Rachel: Oh, that's a nice idea. And will it be the same person every time? Daniel: Yes, we try to keep the same sitter for the whole booking, and we nearly always manage it. Rachel: Great. Well, I'd like to go ahead and book, then. Daniel: Wonderful. Can I start with your name, please? Rachel: Yes, it's Rachel Dunmore. That's D, U, N, M, O, R, E. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a consultant talking to a group of restaurant owners about reducing food waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Good afternoon, everyone. My name's Claire Hollins, and for the past eight years I've been working with restaurants and cafés to help them cut down on the amount of food they throw away. I'm sure you've all seen how much food ends up in the bin at the end of a busy night. And I'm sure most of you would like to see less of it. Speaker: So where does all this waste come from? When I ask restaurant owners, most of them say it's food that goes off in the fridge or the store room before it can be used. Others say it's the trimmings and peelings from preparing vegetables and meat in the kitchen. Both of those are real, of course. But what most owners don't realise is that the biggest share of the waste in a typical restaurant is the food that customers leave on their plates. Speaker: So what does all this waste actually mean for you as owners? Well, some people worry that it'll get them a bad reputation, or that it'll cause problems when the council inspectors come round. In practice, that very rarely happens. The real impact is on your costs. Every plate of food that goes in the bin is food you've paid for, and paid staff to prepare, and then paid again to have taken away. Over a year, that can add up to thousands of pounds. Speaker: So, what can you do about it? First, let's get rid of one very common mistake. Whatever you do, never throw food away simply because it's passed its best before date. That date is about quality, not safety. Food is often perfectly good for some time afterwards, so check it and use it. It's the use by date that you must take seriously, and of course you should always follow the rules on storing food at the right temperature. But far too much good food is wasted because of a misunderstanding about those labels. Speaker: Cutting waste can bring other benefits too, some of which you might not expect. Take The Harbour Kitchen, a seafood restaurant down on the seafront. When they started looking at what was coming back from the tables, they realised their main courses were simply too big, so they reduced the portion sizes. They expected to save money on ingredients, and they did. What they hadn't predicted, though, was that far more diners started ordering a dessert, because they weren't too full to manage one. So their takings per table actually went up. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Now I'd like to give you some examples of restaurants I've worked with recently, to show you some of the different approaches that are possible. Speaker: At The Olive Tree, the owner realised that her staff didn't see food waste as their problem at all. So now, at the end of every evening, the kitchen team weigh the bins themselves and write the figure on a board, and once a month they all sit down together to discuss ideas for bringing the number down. Several of the best ideas have come from the youngest members of staff. Speaker: Café Lumo is a small bakery café in the city centre. They always had bread and cakes left over at the end of the day, which were thrown away. Now a local charity sends a volunteer to collect anything that hasn't been sold, and it's taken to a night shelter for homeless people. The café's waste has dropped enormously. Speaker: The Brasserie used to have a menu with more than forty dishes. That meant keeping a huge range of ingredients in stock, and many of them went off before anyone ordered them. The chef cut the menu down to fifteen dishes that share a lot of the same ingredients, and their waste has fallen by about a third. Speaker: Spice Garden, an Indian restaurant, had a different problem, which was the vegetable peelings and scraps from the kitchen. They now have an arrangement with a community garden near the restaurant. The garden's volunteers collect the scraps twice a week and turn them into compost, and in return, the restaurant gets some of the herbs they grow. Speaker: At the Riverside Grill, lots of customers were leaving large amounts of chips and salad on their plates. So they now offer most of their dishes in two portion sizes, regular and light, and they've also stopped serving side dishes automatically. Customers order them if they want them. Speaker: And finally, The Mill House, where the head chef now runs a short course for every new member of kitchen staff. They learn how to store food properly, how to use every part of a vegetable, and how to turn leftovers into staff meals. Speaker: OK, so now I'd like to move on to look at some of the costs involved. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two product design students called Leo and Hannah talking about Leo's interest in cooking and about a seminar on the history of kitchen equipment. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Hannah: Hi, Leo. So, how are you finding the course so far? Leo: Really well, thanks. Hannah: I've been meaning to ask you. Someone told me you were planning to be a chef when you were at school. Is that right? Leo: That's right. From about the age of fourteen, that was all I wanted to do. I cooked all the time. Hannah: Were you good at it? Leo: Well, everyone in my class seemed to think so. Whenever there was a party, they'd all ask me to make the food, and they'd tell me I should have my own restaurant one day. I loved that, to be honest. Hannah: I'm not surprised. And your family? Did they want you to do something more academic? Leo: No, not at all. My parents were really supportive. My mum used to let me take over the kitchen every weekend. Hannah: So what went wrong? Leo: Looking back, I relied too much on what my friends said. I could make a few impressive dishes, but I never really bothered to learn the basics properly, things like knife skills and making stocks and sauces. I should have spent a lot more time on those. Hannah: Didn't your teachers tell you that? Leo: They probably tried. Anyway, when I was seventeen, I got a place on a work experience scheme in a restaurant in Lyon, in France, for a week. It was a really well-known restaurant. I was so excited before I went. But on the first morning, the head chef asked me to make a simple omelette. He took one look at it, and threw it in the bin in front of the whole kitchen. Hannah: Oh no. How did you feel? Leo: I just wanted the floor to open up and swallow me. My face went completely red. And he was right. It wasn't good enough. Hannah: Were you angry with him? Leo: No, I wasn't angry, it was fair. And actually, during the rest of the week, I got to see how he worked. The kitchen was incredibly busy, but he never raised his voice, and he noticed every tiny detail. I just thought, that's what a real chef is like. I really looked up to him. Hannah: And were you on your own the whole time? That must have been hard. Leo: I thought I'd be lonely, because I didn't know anyone, but the other kitchen staff took me out every evening, so it was fine. And I expected to be bored, because I spent hours peeling vegetables, but there was always something interesting going on around me. Hannah: So is that why you gave up the idea of being a chef? Leo: Partly. I realised I was more interested in how kitchens work, the equipment and the layout, than in cooking itself. That's how I ended up doing product design. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Hannah: Well, that fits in nicely with our seminar next week, doesn't it? We've got to present some ideas on the history of kitchen equipment. Leo: Yes, I've started making some notes. I thought we could begin with the tin can. It was invented in about eighteen ten, so that food could be kept for a long time, especially for soldiers and sailors. Hannah: But how did they open them? Weren't the early cans made of really thick metal? Leo: Yes, and that's the interesting thing. The can opener wasn't invented until nearly fifty years later. Before that, people had to use a hammer and chisel, or a knife, or even a bayonet. Hannah: That's amazing. OK, what about the electric kettle? That must have been a big improvement on boiling water on a stove. Leo: You'd think so. But the first ones, in the eighteen nineties, had the heating element in a separate compartment underneath the water. They took over ten minutes to boil, so a lot of people didn't see the point of them. Hannah: Right. And then there's the fridge. I read that the early electric ones were very expensive. Leo: They were, but the more serious problem was the gases they used for cooling. Some of them were toxic, like ammonia, and if a fridge leaked, people in the house could become seriously ill. Hannah: I didn't know that. What about the microwave oven? Everyone knows the story about the scientist who found that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted, so I don't think we need to go over that. Leo: No. But what I found surprising was the size of the first ones. The first microwave oven, in nineteen forty-seven, was taller than a person and weighed more than three hundred kilos. It was far too big for an ordinary home kitchen. Anyway, what about non-stick pans? Do you know anything about those? Hannah: Yes, I looked them up. The non-stick coating was created in a laboratory in the nineteen thirties. And in the nineteen fifties, a French engineer was using it on his fishing equipment, to stop his lines getting tangled. It was his wife who suggested he try it on her cooking pans. Leo: That's a great story. And were people suspicious of them at first? Hannah: Apparently not. They sold really well right from the beginning. Leo: OK. And one more, perhaps. The dishwasher? Hannah: Yes, the first really practical one was designed in the eighteen eighties by a woman who was fed up with her servants breaking her china. But for a long time, hardly any families had one. They were mostly bought by hotels and restaurants, and it was decades before they became common in people's homes. Leo: Great. I think we've got plenty for the seminar now. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a food science student giving a presentation about the production of vanilla. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Good morning, everyone. In this series of presentations, we've been looking at natural food products, and today I'm going to talk about vanilla. Most of us know it as a flavour, and many people think of it as rather plain and ordinary. We even use the word vanilla in English to mean something boring. But as you'll see, the story of how it's produced is anything but boring. Student: So, what exactly is vanilla? Well, it comes from the long, thin seed pods of a particular kind of orchid. The pods contain thousands of tiny black seeds, and it's these pods, once they've been treated, that give us the flavour. Vanilla is used in ice cream, cakes, chocolate and drinks, of course, but it's also an important ingredient in many perfumes, because of its warm, sweet smell. And it's a valuable crop. In fact, after saffron, vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world, and I'll explain why in a few minutes. Student: Let's start with the plant itself. The vanilla orchid is a climbing vine, which means it can't support its own weight. In the wild, it grows up the trunks of trees, and on farms it's usually trained to climb up trees or wooden posts. It needs a warm, humid climate, with plenty of rain, but it doesn't like too much direct sunlight, so it needs partial shade to grow well. Today, vanilla is grown in several tropical countries, but by far the largest producer is Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, which grows around four fifths of the world's supply. Student: But vanilla doesn't come from Madagascar originally. It was first grown by the Totonac people in what is now Mexico, many centuries ago. They used it as a flavouring and as a medicine, and later the Aztecs used it to flavour a chocolate drink. When the Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, they took vanilla back to Europe, where it quickly became fashionable. Student: Now, in the following centuries, people tried to grow vanilla in other parts of the world. The plants grew perfectly well, and they produced flowers, but they didn't produce any pods at all. Nobody could understand why. The reason, it turned out, was that the insects that pollinated the flowers in Mexico didn't exist anywhere else. Without them, the flowers simply dropped off. Student: The problem was finally solved in eighteen forty-one, on the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, by a twelve-year-old enslaved boy called Edmond Albius. He discovered that he could pollinate the flowers by hand, using a small stick to lift a thin flap inside the flower and then pressing the parts together with his thumb. It was quick and simple, and it worked. Remarkably, this is still the method used on vanilla farms today, almost two centuries later. Student: So let's look at how vanilla is produced now. Vanilla vines usually start to flower about three years after they're planted. The flowers grow in groups, but each individual flower opens for just one day, usually early in the morning. If it isn't pollinated that day, it won't produce a pod, so workers have to check every plant each morning during the flowering season. A skilled worker can pollinate well over a thousand flowers in a day. This is one of the reasons why vanilla is so expensive: almost every pod in the world has been produced by hand. Student: After pollination, the pods take around nine months to grow to their full size. At this stage they're green and have no smell or flavour at all. Farmers wait until the tips of the pods start to turn yellow, and that's the sign that they're ready to be picked. Picking them too early is a common problem, because vanilla is sometimes stolen from the vines, and some farmers harvest early to protect their crop. But unripe pods produce vanilla of much poorer quality. Student: Once the pods have been picked, the curing process begins, and this is what creates the flavour. First, the pods are dipped in hot water for a few minutes, which stops them from ripening any further. Then they're wrapped in blankets and packed into wooden boxes, where they're left to sweat overnight. Over the following weeks, the pods are spread out in the sun for a few hours each day, and wrapped up again each night. Gradually they turn a deep brown colour, and the typical vanilla smell develops. Student: Finally, the pods are dried slowly indoors for several months. Good quality pods are soft and shiny, and sometimes tiny white crystals appear on their surface. These are crystals of vanillin, which is the main flavour compound. Altogether, the process from flower to finished pod can take well over a year, and that's before the vanilla has even left the farm. So that's the basic process. Now, I'd like to look at the market for vanilla. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
